newsitem.title: FRANCE: French try to hijack Blair aura to woo voters.
newsitem.headline: French try to hijack Blair aura to woo voters.

text.p: French politicians on both left and right are trying to hijack the winning aura of British opposition Labour leader Tony Blair to woo voters in their own parliamentary elections.

The centre-right coalition says the moderate market-oriented policies of Blair's "New Labour", widely expected to sweep Britain's general election on Thursday, are in stark contrast to a more radical platform of France's opposition Socialists, whom they portray as hostages to the Communists.
Socialist Party spokesman Francois Hollande grumbled on Monday that the French right "want to make us believe that the victory of Tony Blair will be a win for conservatives.
"It will be a victory for a leftist party," he said.

Conservative French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette praised Blair as speaking a "language infinitely more modern and, deep down, more in line with the realities of this world" than France's Socialist Party.

"It's really two different worlds," he said in a radio interview, pointing to French Socialist plans to create 700,000 subsidised jobs "at the drop of a hat" if they win the National Assembly election on May 25-June 1.
Labour has embraced privatisation and pledged to abandon tax-and-spend economic policies if they oust Prime Minister John Major after 18 years of Conservative rule. Polls give Blair a huge lead.

The French Socialists say they will halt privatisations, including Air France and France Telecom, and cut the working week gradually to 35 hours from 39 with no loss in pay. They have promised they will not increase taxes but shift the burden from wages to investment income.
"The French left is much more archaic than the British left, the French right is not as liberal as in Britain," said Dominique Moisi, a director of the French Institute of International Relations.

He said the French Socialists were hampered by links to the Communist Party, especially over Europe. The Socialists favour a single European currency from 1999 on certain conditions, while the Communists are bitterly opposed.
The Socialists are more pro-European than either Blair or Major, who have adopted a wait-and-see attitude to the euro.

No French government has undertaken the sweeping capitalist reforms implemented by former prime minister Margaret Thatcher, who freed market forces in the 1980s, bolstering competitiveness but emasculating trade unions and weakening job security.

The left in France says conservative President Jacques Chirac is tempted to follow suit, taking a knife to public spending in the name of "freeing enterprise". But Chirac ruled out a shift to "laisser faire" economics in calling the poll.
France's only avowed Thatcherite, former finance minister Alain Madelin, has been excluded from the front ranks of the centre-right campaign.
"It will be pretty funny if British voters turn to Labour just as the French conservatives want in many ways to copy the model of Thatcherism," Hollande said.
"French right-wing politicians always prefer socialism elsewhere," he joked. For them "there's no better socialist than a German socialist, a British or a Scandinavian socialist".
Hollande said he expected some kind of gesture by Blair to help the French Socialists if Labour wins.

Major is trailing in polls despite robust growth and low unemployment. In France, Prime Minister Alain Juppe's centre-right coalition is leading in the polls despite spluttering growth and record unemployment.
Pierre Lellouche, a foreign policy expert in Chirac's conservative party, described the French left as "dinosaurs...In Britain, there are two conservative parties".
Moisi said the ruling French coalition was far from imitating Thatcher's union-busting policies. The centre-right has frequently backed down in the face of street protests.
Last year, Juppe bowed to demands by truck drivers to retire at 55 instead of 60 after they blocked roads. Wildcat stoppages that would be illegal in Britain disrupt France daily.

Public sector employees make up almost a quarter of the workforce in France against 14 percent in Britain. Every French village has a bakery, a pharmacy and a grocery -- corner shops that have largely been driven out of business by supermarkets in free-market Britain.
